title: Scheduler / Interrupt Affinity: io_uring probe and tiny-request parse jitter
body:
Purpose:
Exploratory notes on an observed jitter pattern on sub-10ms tiny requests. Hypothesis: kernel interrupt handling (NAPI/IRQ affinity) + user-space scheduler placement for Python worker threads causes occasional parse/tokenize path stalls. We probe io_uring vs epoll, IRQ/softirq affinity, and setthreadaffinity to measure impact.

Background / motivation:
- Several production traces show 95th/99th spikes on tiny requests (payload < 200 bytes) even when GPUs are idle and model generation is tiny.
- Previous tokenization deep dives ruled out the tokenizer itself being the dominant cost for median requests; tail shows spikes that line up with kernel scheduling windows.
- Newer kernels and our migration to io_uring (experimental) changed interrupt path; want to validate whether network interrupt offload + thread placement helps for tiny fast-paths.

Quick summary of experiments run (high level):
1) Baseline (epoll + default IRQ affinity): p95 ~= 8.9ms, p99 ~= 27.2ms on microbench (100k tiny requests across 8 cores).
2) Set CPU affinity for request worker threads to cores 2-5, IRQs pinned to cores 0-1: p95 drop to 7.4ms, p99 to 18.9ms.
3) io_uring (liburing v2.4) with submission queue polling enabled, IRQs pinned same: p95 6.8ms, p99 11.3ms.
4) io_uring + offload RX processing (NAPI steering) + worker cores moved to separate NUMA node: p95 7.1ms, p99 14.7ms (worse on p99 due to cross-node memory).

Commands / probes used:
- perf record -a -g -F 4000 -- sleep 30 (on load generator host)
- bpftrace one-liners to sample softirq and kworker wakeups:
  - trace softirq: 'tracepoint:irq:irq_handler_entry { @[comm] = count(); }'
- simple netcat-based microbench harness (tiny-json) that fires async POSTs with keepalive to the serving node.
- strace on fast worker: strace -f -tt -P /var/run/worker.sock -e trace=network,read,write
- setaffinity script: taskset -c 2-5 ./worker

Notable flamegraph observations (from perf + Brendan Gregg script):
- Baseline p99 sample: ~30% cycles in kernel path: __napi_poll -> napi_gro_receive -> net_rx_action -> softirq processing.
- Userland: significant time in syscall enter/exit overheads around recvmsg/sendmsg. Some samples show Python GIL-release gaps during recvmsg leading to scheduler preemption.
- After pinning IRQs to dedicated cores we saw kernel-side softirq hotpath move off our worker cores, resulting in fewer user-space preemptions.

Numbers (microbench run details):
- Hardware: c6i.8xlarge-like. 8 physical cores exposed to guest; hyperthreading off for experiment.
- Harness: 100k requests over 60s, concurrency 64, payload 120 bytes, keep-alive enabled.
- Baseline stats (epoll): median 2.5ms, p95 8.9ms, p99 27.2ms, max 180ms.
- After IRQ-pin + affinity: median 2.4ms, p95 7.4ms, p99 18.9ms, max 92ms.
- io_uring + submit polling: median 2.2ms, p95 6.8ms, p99 11.3ms, max 46ms.

Interpretation so far:
- A large slice of p99 appears correlated with kernel softirq handling interleaving with our worker thread scheduling. When NIC/softirq handling occupies the same cores as the worker, we get preemption and syscalls take longer.
- io_uring with SQ/Poll reduces syscall context switches and can push more of the fast-path into polled user-space, reducing kernel-entry overhead.
- NUMA placement matters: moving workers away from NIC-affinitized cores can reduce interference, but cross-node memory effects can negate gains if data paths touch remote memory.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Are we seeing similar patterns on baremetal with latest drivers? (cloud VMs may have additional virtualization interrupts) — need to run on a staging baremetal node (SRV-987 ticket).
- For Python process model: would moving to more single-threaded async workers (uvloop + aiohttp) with careful event-loop polling outperform our threaded model for tiny requests? (run microbench comparing gunicorn threads vs uvloop single process).
- What's the overhead of enabling io_uring submit-poll in our code path with heavy TLS/SSL libraries? Do we need TLS offload to keep latency low?
- Can we use SO_RXQ_OVFL or BPF to mark/steer tiny requests to a fast-path queue to avoid generic processing?

Hypothesis-driven experiments to run next:
1) Native baremetal run with same harness and capture perf+tracepoints. Compare with VM runs to isolate virtualization interrupts. (owner: @Priya)
2) Controlled CPU topology test matrix: all cores shared vs isolated IRQ cores vs ht on/off. Measure p50/p95/p99 and tail shapes. (owner: @Ethan)
3) Python runtime variants: threaded worker (current), multi-process with cpu affinity, single-process uvloop. Instrument GIL hold times (pyflame/profiler) to see if preemption is GIL-related. (owner: @Sofia)
4) Microkernel-level: try bpf program to count softirq to CPU and correlate with request timestamps to directly link softirq bursts to request spikes. (owner: @Arjun)
5) Try a disabled preemption test: set sched_{fifo|rr} for worker threads to observe behavior (only as lab test, not production).

Quick notes on mitigations to try if pattern confirmed:
- Pin networking IRQs to dedicated cores and reserve worker cores without IRQs (we saw good gains in p99).
- Enable io_uring with submit polling on serving sockets for tiny-request hot-path, fall back to epoll for larger streaming paths.
- Introduce local shared NVMe-based ingress queue with userland poller (experimental), to isolate network interrupt variability.
- Recommend region-level machine type selection that supports MSI-X steering and good NIC drivers for production tiny-request customers.

Risks / constraints:
- io_uring SQ/poll consumes CPU while polling; need to measure cost under sustained load (we saw ~3% CPU increase but 40% p99 improvement).
- IRQ pinning requires admin privileges and might be brittle on autoscaling instances. Need automation in init scripts and safe defaults.
- Changing Python runtime model is invasive and interacts with existing tracing & observability (we must preserve request tracing across process boundaries).

Quick reproduction checklist (how to reproduce locally):
1) Launch instance with kernel 6.1+ (recommended) or our internal staging image.
2) Build liburing and enable io_uring in our worker binary (--use-io-uring flag).
3) Run harness: ./microbench -c 64 -n 100000 -p tiny.json --keepalive target:8080
4) Attach perf while running and collect: perf record -a -g -F 4000 -- sleep 60
5) Run flamegraph script: perf script | ./stackcollapse-perf.pl | ./flamegraph.pl > out.svg

Notes-to-self / hypotheses to annotate into Confluence:
- Add a section highlighting kernel-level interference as a first-class cause of tiny-request tails (not just tokenization algorithmic cost).
- Provide recommended AMI images and an init step to set IRQ affinity for dedicated inference pools.

Unresolved observations from recent run (2025-09-30):
- One outlier p99 (~180ms) in baseline trace included a ksoftirqd busy-loop that coincided with a simultaneous background snapshotting job on the host (disk interrupts). This suggests that non-NIC interrupts (disk/timer) can also introduce spikes.

References/links (internal + external):
- Linux NAPI and softirq docs: https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/networking/napi.html
- io_uring polling benefits: https://lwn.net/Articles/806922/
- GH PR with prototype changes: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/1423
- Jira ticket for baremetal runs: SRV-987

Next check-in:
- Will run baremetal reproduction (owner: Priya) and share perf flamegraphs + bpftrace dumps by 2025-10-07. Follow-up plan: if consistent improvements, start drafting an ops-runbook for IRQ pinning + io_uring opt-in for tiny-request customer tiers.

Notes: this document is intentionally a scratchpad — many loose threads, please add observations inline.
